# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-22 (Extended v161)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (Lamarque's funeral procession and ensuing riots, mid-June 1832)**: Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house with secret passage to Rue de Babylone), Place de la Bastille (elephant monument), Prison Chargemagne, Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile (ruin wall), Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire No. 6 (Gillenormand residence), Champ-de-Mars, esplanade of bridge of Austerlitz, Quai Bourdon, Boulevard Bourdon, Rue Bassompierre, Isle Louviers timber-yards, Rue Saint-Pierre-Montmartre, Rue des Jeûneurs, Rue du Cadran, Rue Montorgueil, Rue Mandar, Boulevard Saint-Martin, Rue Beaubourg, Rue Michel-le-Comte, Rue du Temple, Quai de la Grève, Latin quarter, Halles district, Quartier Saint-Jacques, Rue Saint-Hyacinthe, Café du Progrès, Rue des Mathurins, Café des Sept-Billards, Rue Transnonain, Rue Sainte-Avoye, Rue Simon-Le-Franc, Rue de la Corderie, Rue du Cimitière-Saint-Nicolas, English provincial towns (Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford, Gulhaven, Kelmere). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 (frost, rain, thunder, muddy roads, early darkness) transitioned to spring Year 6 (cholera decimated Paris), now summer Year 6 (flat smoke over fields, bees in lavender, threats of rain, ruts and puddles from thaw, salt-and-tar smells from water). **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately—unverified. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Fenelle Lindmere confided Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified. **Rumor (spring Year 6)**: Second daughter of Rorald Lindmere spread rumor Pelde Stenworth died of plague—unverified. **Late night claim (earlier summer Year 6)**: Youngest son of Ludrek Prydenridge confided to Isric Thornmere that old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar—unverified.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (Autumn Year 5—Mid-June 1832)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn (origin unclear). Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself entirely to his care. Recovered through March-April.

**Mysterious journeys and nocturnal manuscript**: Valjean took occasional journeys of one or two days, destination unknown to Cosette, typically when money lacking. Cosette observed figure walking in garden dusk carrying large club. Found stone on bench; became alarmed. Later discovered packet of philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark. **Cosette recognized writer as Marius.**

**Imminent departure (late June 1832)**: Valjean told Cosette morning of 24th June that he must settle all affairs; hold herself in readiness; he will give her linen to pack in trunk; obliged to go on journey; they are to go away; large trunk needed for her and small one for him. All to be ready in one week. **Possible destination: England.**

**Thénardier sighting (spring Year 6 through summer Year 6)**: While walking on boulevard, Valjean caught sight of Thénardier; thanks to disguise (workman's waistcoat, gray linen trousers, long-visored cap), Thénardier did not recognize him. Since that day, Valjean has seen him repeatedly; now certain Thénardier prowling about their neighborhood. Valjean now rarely goes out with Cosette; spends time alone meditating on isolated slopes of Champ-de-Mars.

**Mysterious figure (spring Year 6)**: While sitting on back of solitary slope in Champ-de-Mars, Valjean perceived creature larger than child, not so large as man, clad in gray blouse and dust-colored cotton velvet trousers, jumping over parapet and slipping into moat. Identity unclear.

**Political unease**: Paris not tranquil; political troubles cause police to grow very uneasy and suspicious. While seeking men like Pépin or Morey, they might readily discover man like Jean Valjean.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (Autumn Year 5—Evening 24th June 1832)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never truly forgotten Marius, had always loved and adored him. "Fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it burst forth afresh, and inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter and nature of love**: Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening after recognizing house through Éponine's assistance. Entered garden by forcing old gate; being slender, readily passed through. **At height of love's voluptuousness, Marius remained absolutely chaste.** Love described as "chaste, almost shy" yet not devoid of gallantry. Their conversations made of breaths, murmurs, whispers, childish prattle, laughter at nothing.

**Confessions of identity (spring Year 6)**: **Cholera decimated Paris during that month.** They confided as far as possible, but not much further than names. **Marius told Cosette**: orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, lived by writing for publishers, father was colonel and hero, on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. **Cosette told Marius**: brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father's name M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave greatly to poor despite being poor himself.

**Marius's response and last arrangement (late June 1832)**: For last six weeks, Marius slowly taken possession of Cosette. **Upon learning of Valjean's plan to take Cosette to England in one week**: Marius declared this gravest atrocity imaginable. **Protested he has no money (owes more than ten louis to Courfeyrac), old hat worth three francs, coat missing buttons, shirt ragged, elbows torn, boots leak, cannot afford passport.** Cosette agreed not to question further, accepted Marius as her master. **Arranged to meet in garden day after tomorrow (26th June) at nine o'clock precisely at dusk.** Both fell into each other's arms, lips meeting while uplifted eyes gazed upon stars.

**Marius's despair (evening 24th June 1832)**: Approached grating to garden. Displaced bar and rushed headlong into garden. Cosette was not at ordinary waiting spot. Traversed thicket, approached recess near flight of steps—not there. Raised eyes; shutters of house closed. Made tour of garden; garden deserted. Returned to house and knocked repeatedly on shutters. Called "Cosette!" imperiously. No reply. All was over; no one in garden; no one in house. **Fixed despairing eyes on dismal house, black and silent as tomb. Gazed at stone seat where he had passed adorable hours with Cosette. Seated himself on flight of steps, heart filled with sweetness and resolution. Blessed his love in depths of thought, said to himself that since Cosette was gone, all that was left for him was to die.**

**Marius carries pistols (spring Year 6 through summer Year 6)**: Took pistols which Javert gave him at time of 3d February adventure; they remained in his hands and remained loaded. **Summer Year 6: Put pistols in his pocket and went out with Enjolras, Feuilly, and Combeferre, all ready to go out. Vague thought he had in mind when taking them unclear.**

## Father Gillenormand and Marius's Return (Late June 1832)
**Character and state**: Well past ninety-first birthday. Lives with Mademoiselle Gillenormand in Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6. Incapable of taking single step towards grandson; would rather die. Placed old portrait of other daughter (dead), Madame Pontmercy, taken when eighteen, opposite head of bed—gazed incessantly at it.

**Evening of 24th June 1832 (before Marius's final arrival)**: Alone in chamber, feet propped on andirons, half enveloped in huge screen of coromandel lacquer, elbow on table where burned two candles under green shade. Thinking of Marius lovingly and bitterly; bitterness predominated. Tenderness once soured always ended by boiling and turning to indignation. Trying to accustom himself to thought that all was over; whole nature revolted; aged paternity would not consent.

**Marius's arrival and awkward reunion (after four years)**: Gillenormand grasped Marius in single glance. Found him noble, handsome, distinguished, well-grown, complete man. Felt desire to open his arms, call him, fling himself forward; heart melted with rapture. But by contrast which constituted foundation of his nature, what came forth was harshness. Marius responded with coldness, causing goodman unendurable and irritating anxiety.

**Harsh interrogation and announcement**: Gillenormand delivered bitter diatribe comparing youth's advantages to old man's infirmities. Demanded to know why Marius deserted him. **Announced he would marry.** Gillenormand reacted with fury. **Upon learning her name related to Fauchelevent, declared absolutely: "Never, sir, never!"**

**Sudden reversal and Marius's confession**: At tone of "never," Marius lost all hope, traversed chamber with slow steps, tottering like dying man. At moment Marius on point of going out, Gillenormand advanced with senile vivacity, seized him by collar, brought him back energetically, flung him into armchair. There was now something so kind, so gentle, so openhearted, and so paternal in this brusqueness that Marius, in sudden transition from discouragement to hope, was stunned and intoxicated. **Marius passionately declared love for Cosette, described meeting her at Luxembourg, seeing her every day at her home, her father's planned departure to England, his desperation without her.** Stated: "She lives in a garden with an iron fence, in the Rue Plumet. It is in the neighborhood of the Invalides."

**Gillenormand's dangerous response and misrecognition (late June 1832)**: Seated near table, light from candles brought out dilapidation of Marius's costume, which Gillenormand regarded with amazement. Gillenormand, while listening and drinking in sound of Marius's voice, enjoyed protracted pinch of snuff. **At words "Rue Plumet" Gillenormand interrupted his inhalation and allowed remainder of snuff to fall upon his knees.** **Delivered rambling response containing reference to "Rue Blomet, Pamela, barracks, lancer," which passed before Marius like dissolving view, appearing to have nothing to do with Cosette.** **Gillenormand appeared to wander in his mind, but terminated rambling in words which Marius understood and which were mortal insult to Cosette: "make her your mistress."** **Those words entered heart of strict young man like sword.** Octogenarian raised hands to temples with expression of anguish, recoiled tottering, fell back into armchair, pulseless, voiceless, tearless, with quivering head and lips which moved with stupid air, with nothing in eyes and nothing in heart except gloomy and profound something resembling night. **However, Marius was at age when one believes nothing in line of evil. Suspicions are wrinkles; early youth has none. Suspect Cosette! There are hosts of crimes Marius could sooner have committed.** Gillenormand's dangerous mischaracterization left no trace in Marius's mind; not slightest.

## Éponine's Guardianship (Spring Year 6)
**Éponine guards Rue Plumet house against intruders.** On evening of 3d June 1832, towards ten o'clock, confronts unknown parties (possibly Thénardier and associates): tells them she is there; forbids anyone to enter house; claims she is dog and will bark; says six men don't frighten her; threatens kicks; displays resolute attitude with elbow on knee, chin in hand, swinging foot with indifference.

## Thénardier's Escape and Accomplices (Winter Year 5)
**Thénardier's escape from Prison Chargemagne**: At two o'clock morning, old sentinel relieved by conscript. At four o'clock, relieving sentinel found conscript asleep. **Thénardier vanished. Hole in cage ceiling and above in roof. One bed plank wrenched off. Half-empty bottle with stupefying wine seized. Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** Reached edge of ruin wall but strength failed him.

**Four ruffians' vigil and Gavroche's role**: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, and Montparnasse prowled all night around La Force. **Guelemer seized Gavroche, set him on roof of shanty, handed him rope knotted by Brujon. Gavroche directed steps towards flue. Thénardier bent over wall edge; first light of dawn struck white upon his sweat-dripping brow. Gavroche recognized him.** Brujon and Guelemer successfully escaped.

## Gavroche and the Two Lost Children (Spring 1832—Spring Year 6)
**Character and rescue**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Stole Montparnasse's purse. Observed two neatly dressed children; barber thrust them back furiously. Gavroche provided bread and promised shelter.

**Elephant shelter**: Led two children through fence gap into elephant enclosure. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5.

## M. Mabeuf's Destitution (Spring Year 6—4th June 1832)
**Character and losses**: Venerable old man of austerity and learning. Received Jean Valjean's purse (from Gavroche via starry mythology) but in infantile austerity did not accept it as gift; took it to police commissioner as lost article. No one claimed it. Purse did not succor him. Age eighty.

**Book sales to survive**: Forced to sell library, volume by volume, to second-hand dealers for pittance. Sold books for 20 sous when purchased for 20 francs. Cherished secret hope he would die before finishing selling books. Once sold Robert Estienne for 35 sous, bought Aldus for 40 sous—owed 5 sous, beamed with joy to Mother Plutarque, had no dinner.

**Horticultural Society and humiliation**: Belonged to Horticultural Society; destitution became known. President promised to speak to Minister of Agriculture and Commerce; Minister said old savant must be helped. Received invitation to dine with Minister. Went trembling with joy. Perceived ragged cravat, long square coat, waxed shoes astonished ushers. No one spoke to him. Heard Minister's wife (beautiful, low-necked gown) inquire: "Who is that old gentleman?" Returned home on foot at midnight in driving rain-storm. Had sold Elzevir to pay for carriage.

**Final sacrifice (4th June 1832)**: Mother Plutarque fell ill; needed expensive potion and nurse. Bookcase contained nothing; last volume departed. Only Diogenes Laertius remained. Put unique copy under arm, went to Porte Saint-Jacques to Royal's successor, returned with one hundred francs. Laid pile of five-franc pieces on old serving-woman's nightstand, returned to chamber without saying word.

**Aftermath (morning after 4th June)**: Seated himself on overturned post in garden at dawn, motionless over hedge, head drooping, eyes vaguely fixed on withered flower-beds. Rained at intervals; old man did not perceive.

## Lamarque's Funeral Procession and Ensuing Riots (Mid-June 1832)
**General Lamarque**: Man of renown and action. Had bravery requisite for Empire and Restoration—bravery of battlefield and tribune. Eloquent as valiant; sword discernible in speech. Like Foy, upheld liberty after command; sat between left and extreme left; beloved of people accepting chances of future; beloved of populace because served Emperor well; one of Napoleon's marshals _in petto_ with Comtes Gérard and Drouet. Treaties of 1815 removed him as personal offence. Hated Wellington with hatred pleasing multitude. For seventeen years majestically preserved sadness of Waterloo. In death agony clasped to breast sword presented by officers of Hundred Days. Napoleon died uttering word "army"; Lamarque uttering word "country." Death occurred mid-June 1832.

**Government military response**: Government observed with hand on sword. Four squadrons carabineers in Place Louis XV with trumpets, filled cartridge-boxes, loaded muskets ready to march. Municipal Guard echelonned in Latin country and Jardin des Plantes. Squadron dragoons at Halle-aux-Vins. Half of 12th Light Infantry at Grève, other half at Bastille. 6th Dragoons at Célestins. Louvre courtyard full of artillery. Remainder troops confined to barracks; regiments in environs of Paris. Power uneasy, held suspended twenty-four thousand soldiers in city and thirty thousand in banlieue over menacing multitude.

**Funeral procession (mid-June 1832)**: Legitimist tricks hinted at; spoke of Duc de Reichstadt whom God marked for death when populace designated him for Empire. Unknown personage announced two overseers would throw open doors of factory of arms to people. Majority of uncovered brows showed enthusiasm mingled with dejection. Procession proceeded with feverish slowness from deceased's house via boulevards to Bastille. Rained from time to time; throng undeterred. Coffin borne round Vendome column, stones thrown at Duc de Fitz-James on balcony with hat on head, Gallic cock torn from popular flag dragged in mire, policeman wounded with sword blow at Porte Saint-Martin, officer 12th Light Infantry declaring aloud "I am a Republican," Polytechnic School coming unexpectedly against orders, shouts "Long live Polytechnique! Long live Republic!" marked passage of funeral train. At Bastille, long files of curious formidable people descended from Faubourg Saint-Antoine, effected junction with procession, certain terrible seething began agitating throng.

**Hearse at Austerlitz bridge esplanade**: Hearse passed Bastille, traversed small bridge, reached esplanade of bridge of Austerlitz. There it halted. Crowd would have presented aspect of comet whose head was on esplanade and whose tail spread out over Quai Bourdon, covered Bastille, and was prolonged on boulevard as far as Porte Saint-Martin. Circle traced around hearse. Vast rout held their peace. **Lafayette spoke and bade Lamarque farewell. This was touching and august instant, all heads uncovered, all hearts beat high.** Red flag raised storm and disappeared in midst of it. From Boulevard Bourdon to bridge of Austerlitz one of those clamors which resemble billows stirred multitude. Two prodigious shouts went up: "Lamarque to the Pantheon!—Lafayette to the Town-hall!"

**Dragoon intervention and initial violence (mid-June 1832)**: Young men harnessed themselves and began to drag Lamarque in hearse across bridge of Austerlitz and Lafayette in hackney-coach along Quai Morland. Municipal cavalry on left bank set in motion, came to bar bridge; on right bank dragoons emerged from Célestins and deployed along Quai Morland. Men dragging Lafayette caught sight of dragoons at corner of quay and shouted: "The dragoons!" Dragoons advanced at walk, in silence, with pistols in holsters, swords in scabbards, guns slung in leather sockets, with air of gloomy expectation. Halted two hundred paces from little bridge. Carriage in which sat Lafayette advanced to them; their ranks opened and allowed it to pass, then closed behind it. At that moment dragoons and crowd touched. Women fled in terror. **Dark moment when two clouds come together.** Three shots suddenly discharged: first killed Cholet, chief of squadron; second killed old deaf woman closing her window; third singed shoulder of officer. Woman screamed: "They are beginning too soon!" All at once, squadron of dragoons which had remained in barracks up to this time, was seen to debouch at gallop with bared swords, through Rue Bassompierre and Boulevard Bourdon, sweeping all before them.

**Generalizing of riots**: Tempest loosed, stones rained down, fusillade broke forth, many precipitated themselves to bottom of bank, passed small arm of Seine, timber-yards of Isle Louviers (vast citadel ready to hand) bristled with combatants. Stakes torn up, pistol-shots fired, barricade begun. Young men thrust back passed Austerlitz bridge with hearse at run. Municipal guard, carabineers rushed up; dragoons plied their swords; crowd dispersed in all directions. Rumor of war flew to all four quarters of Paris. Men shouted: "To arms!" ran, tumbled down, fled, resisted. Wrath spread abroad riot as wind spreads fire.

**Spontaneous uprising across Paris**: Nothing more extraordinary than first breaking out of riot. Everything burst forth everywhere at once. Insurrection assumes character of plot in some places; improvisation in others. Shops closed, merchant displays disappeared. Isolated shots fired. Blows from gun-stocks beat against doors; servants heard laughing in courtyards saying "There's going to be a row!" Red flags and proclamations carried. Factory of small-arms on Boulevard Saint-Martin pillaged; three armorers' shops plundered (Rue Beaubourg, Rue Michel-le-Comte, Rue du Temple). In few minutes thousand hands seized and carried off two hundred thirty guns (nearly all double-barrelled), sixty-four swords, eighty-three pistols. Young men armed with muskets installed themselves in houses of women to fire from windows; made cartridges. Across right bank, left bank, quays, boulevards, Latin country, quarter of Halles, panting men, artisans, students, members of sections broke street lanterns, unharnessed carriages, unpaved streets, broke in doors of houses, uprooted trees, rummaged cellars, rolled out hogsheads, heaped up paving-stones, rough slabs, furniture and planks, made barricades. Forced bourgeois to assist. Entered dwellings of women, forced them hand over swords and guns of absent husbands, wrote on doors with whiting: "The arms have been delivered"; some signed "their names" to receipts and said: "Send for them to-morrow at the Mayor's office." Disarmed isolated sentinels and National Guardsmen on streets. Tore epaulets from officers. In Rue du Cimitière-Saint-Nicolas, officer of National Guard, pursued by crowd armed with clubs and foils, took refuge with difficulty in house, only able to emerge at nightfall in disguise.

**Student activity**: In Quartier Saint-Jacques students swarmed out of hotels and ascended Rue Saint-Hyacinthe to Café du Progrès, or descended to Café des Sept-Billards in Rue des Mathurins. There, young men mounted on stone corner-posts distributed arms. Plundered timber-yard in Rue Transnonain for barricade material. At corner of Rue Sainte-Avoye and Rue Simon-Le-Franc, inhabitants resisted and destroyed barricade with own hands. At Rue de Temple, insurgents abandoned begun barricade after firing on National Guard detachment, fled through Rue de la Corderie. Detachment picked up red flag, package of cartridges, three hundred pistol-balls. National Guardsmen tore up flag, carried off tattered remains on points of bayonets.

## Provincial Details (Winter Year 5—Summer Year 6)
**Deaths, transfers, births, migrations**: Ulrald Corrford died of old age at Staveford. Silver flute and amber map went to Kassa Brackick. Kassa Stenson gave up idleness and took work as scribe. Kassa Stenson gave youngest son of Gadan Corrley solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Yarlby. **Yewyn Haskick gave birth to son, named Sebin Brackick; father Tatho Brackick; family lives in Salcombe.** **Rovus Prydenridge quit Ostcombe for good and took lodgings in Kelmere (after quarrel).** **Wenelle Lindmere went to live in Kelmere as well (timing: summer Year 6).**

**Characters mentioned**: Vesmira, Luvie Prydenridge, Islan Thornmere, Isvie Stenworth, Marald Corrford, Fenelle Lindmere, Elra Corrford, Yedan Corrford, Ferald Stenworth, Thizek Stenenridge, Luena Stenenridge, Lurald Stenworth, Rorald Lindmere, Pelde Stenworth, Havie, Isric Thornmere, Ludrek Prydenridge, Zavus, Rovus, Gadrek Prydenridge, Kassa Brackick, Taric Corrley, Rimor Corrford, Sebin, Pelia, Nerine, Yera.

**Minor observations (summer Year 6)**: Smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Yera hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Luvie remarked river is up again; Islan Thornmere said it always was in spring. Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar; somewhere dog barked at nothing then went quiet. Fenelle Lindmere fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Lurald Stenworth laughed at story nobody else found funny (mentioned twice). Thizek walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Isric Thornmere counted coins twice and came up penny short (mentioned twice). Nerine counted coins twice and still came up penny short. Isric Thornmere and Nerine talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Price of salt scandal discussed between Rimor Corrford and Kassa. Kassa told Kassa Stenson he looked tired; he did not deny it. Rimor Corrford hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Tatho hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Tatho fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Vesmira Thornmere complained of aching back. Vesmira Thornmere watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Sebin complained of aching back. Yewyn Haskick sorted old letters by candlelight. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Light went early as it did that time of year.
